'''''Dracaena trifasciata''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asparagaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to tropical West Africa from Nigeria east to the Congo. It is most commonly known as the '''snake plant''', '''Saint George's sword''', '''mother-in-law's tongue''' (a name it shares with ''[[Dracaena hyacinthoides]]''), and '''viper's bowstring hemp''', among other names.<ref name="SUBG">{{cite web |title=Sansevieria trifasciata |url=https://sun.gardenexplorer.org/taxon-2175.aspx |publisher=[[Stellenbosch University Botanical Garden]] |access-date=30 July 2019 |language=en |date=20 July 2019 }}</ref> Until 2017, it was known under the [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] ''Sansevieria trifasciata''.<ref name=WCSP/> This plant is often kept as a [[houseplant]] due to its non-demanding maintenance; they can survive with very little water and sun.

==Description==
It is an [[evergreen]]<!--not herbaceous--> [[perennial plant]] forming dense strands, spreading by way of its creeping [[rhizome]], which is sometimes above ground, sometimes underground. Its stiff leaves grow vertically from a basal [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]]. Mature leaves are dark green with light gray-green cross-banding and usually range from {{convert|70|–|90|cm|ft}} long and {{convert|5|–|6|cm|in}} wide, though it can reach heights above {{cvt|6|ft|m|0|order=flip}} in optimal conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Snake Plant |url=https://www.bhg.com/gardening/plant-dictionary/houseplant/snake-plant/ |access-date=15 June 2021 |website=Better Homes & Gardens |language=en }}</ref> 

The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''trifasciata'' means "with three bundles".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=9781845337315 |page=224 }}</ref>

The plant exchanges [[oxygen]] and [[carbon dioxide]] using the [[crassulacean acid metabolism]] process, which allows them to withstand drought. The microscopic pores on the plant's leaves, called the [[stomata]] and used to exchange gases, are opened only at night to prevent water from escaping via [[evaporation]] in the hot sun.

To get this plant to go into bloom outside of its natural environment is difficult. Replicating its natural environment is possible. Its flowers vary from greenish white to cream-colored — some are fragrant at night, others not at all — and have a sticky texture.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Dracaena trifasciata'' Care – #1 Best Care Guide |url=https://plantophiles.com/plant-care/dracaena-trifasciata/ |website=Plantophiles |date=2 January 2021 }}</ref>

''Dracaena trifasciata'' is commonly called "[[Mother-in-law joke|mother-in-law's tongue]]", "[[Saint George and the Dragon|Saint George]]'s sword" or "snake plant", because of the shape and sharp margins of its [[leaf|leaves]]<ref name="SUBG" /> that resemble snakes. It is also known as the "viper's bowstring hemp", because it is one of the sources for [[plant fiber]]s used to make [[bowstring]]s.<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SATR6|taxon=Sansevieria trifasciata|access-date=30 October 2015 }}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
Like other members of its genus, ''D. trifasciata'' yields bowstring hemp, a strong [[plant fiber]] once used to make bowstrings.

It is now used predominantly as an [[ornamental plant]], outdoors in warmer climates, and indoors as a [[houseplant]] in cooler climates. It is popular as a houseplant because it is tolerant of low light levels and irregular watering; during winter, it needs only one watering every few months. It will rot easily if overwatered.<ref name="gthp">{{cite web |url=http://www.guide-to-houseplants.com/mother-in-laws-tongue.html |title=Mother-in-Law's Tongue or Snake Plant |access-date=4 March 2010 }}</ref> It is commonly recommended to beginners interested in cultivating houseplants for its easy care.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.themanual.com/culture/easy-plants-for-beginners/ |website=The Manual |access-date=17 May 2020 |title=The 8 Best Indoor Plants To Buy in 2022 |last=Roscoe |first=Zoe |date=1 October 2021 }}</ref>

The [[NASA Clean Air Study]] found ''D. trifasciata'' has the potential to filter indoor air, removing four of the five main toxins involved in the effects of [[sick building syndrome]].<ref>{{cite report |title=A study of interior landscape plants for indoor air pollution abatement |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19930073077.pdf |author1=BC Wolverton |author2=WL Douglas |author3=K Bounds |date=July 1989 |id=NASA-TM-108061 |publisher=[[NASA]] }}</ref> However, its rate of filtration is too slow for practical indoor use.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cummings |first1=Bryan E. |last2=Waring |first2=Michael S. |date=6 November 2019 |title=Potted plants do not improve indoor air quality: a review and analysis of reported VOC removal efficiencies |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41370-019-0175-9 |journal=Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology |volume=30 |issue=2 |language=en |pages=253–261 |doi=10.1038/s41370-019-0175-9 |pmid=31695112 |s2cid=207911697 |issn=1559-064X |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It can be [[Plant propagation|propagated]] by [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]] or by dividing the rhizome. The first method has the disadvantage that the [[variegation]] will be lost.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/foliage/folnotes/sansevie.htm |title=Sansevieria Production Guide }}</ref>

''D. trifasciata'' is considered by some authorities a potential weed in Australia. It is widely used as an ornamental in the tropics outdoors in pots and garden beds, and in temperate areas as an indoor plant.<ref name="csurhes">{{cite web |url=http://www.weeds.gov.au/publications/books/pubs/potential.pdf |title=Potential environmental weeds in Australia: Candidate species for preventative control |author=S. Csurhes and R. Edwards |year=1998 |publisher=Queensland Department of Natural Resources |access-date=26 March 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071010044320/http://www.weeds.gov.au/publications/books/pubs/potential.pdf |archive-date=10 October 2007 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=mother-in-law's tongue {{!}} Weed Identification – Brisbane City Council |url=https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/mother-laws-tongue |access-date=23 June 2019 |website=weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au }}</ref>{{clear left}}

The plant contains [[saponin]]s which are mildly [[toxic]] to dogs and cats and can lead to gastrointestinal upset if consumed.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants/mother-laws-tongue |title=Mother-in-Law's Tongue |publisher=[[ASPCA]] }}</ref>

In South Africa, it is used to treat ear infections.{{Citation needed|date=April 2024}}

==Varieties and cultivars==

Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been developed, many of them for [[variegation|variegated]] foliage with yellow or silvery-white stripes on the leaf margins. Popular cultivars include 'Compacta', 'Goldiana', 'Hahnii', 'Laurentii', 'Silbersee', and 'Silver Hahnii'. 'Hahnii' was discovered in 1939 by William W. Smith Jr. in the Crescent Nursery Company, [[New Orleans]], Louisiana. The 1941 patent was assigned to Sylvan Frank Hahn of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.<ref>{{cite web |last=Smith |first=William Walter |title=Sansevieria |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/USPP470 |work=Plant Patent 470 |publisher=United States Patent Office |access-date=26 March 2013 }}</ref>

The variety ''D. trifasciata'' var. ''laurentii'',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/97639/Sansevieria-trifasciata-var-laurentii-(v)/Details |title=''Sansevieria trifasciata'' var. ''laurentii'' |publisher=RHS |access-date=18 February 2019 }}</ref> together with the [[cultivar]]s 'Bantel's Sensation'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/103285/Sansevieria-trifasciata-Bantel-s-Sensation/Details |title=''Sansevieria trifasciata'' 'Bantel's Sensation' |publisher=RHS |access-date=18 February 2019 }}</ref> 
and 'Golden Hahni'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/81378/Sansevieria-trifasciata-Golden-Hahnii-(v)/Details |title=''Sansevierie trifasciata'' 'Golden Hahni' |publisher=RHS |access-date=18 February 2019 }}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |title=AGM Plants - Ornamental |date=July 2017 |page=94 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=28 October 2018 }}</ref>

Non-variegated forms of ''D. trifasciata'' are often incorrectly sold as ''[[Dracaena zeylanica|Sansevieria zeylanica]]'', which is a different species that is rarely cultivated.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Newton |first1=L.E. |editor1-last=Eggli |editor1-first=Urs |editor2-last=Nyffeler |editor2-first=R. |title=Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants: Monocotyledons |date=2020 |publisher=Springer-Verlag GmbH |location=Berlin |pages=1353–1385 |edition=2nd |chapter=''Sansevieria'' RUSCACEAE }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Henley |first1=R.W. |last2=Chase |first2=A.R. |last3=Osborne |first3=L.S. |title=''Sansevieria'' Production Guide (CFREC-A Foliage Plant Note RH-91-30) |url=https://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/foliage/folnotes/sansevie.htm |access-date=8 February 2023 }}</ref>

==Cultural significance==
In its native range in Africa, ''Dracaena trifasciata'' specimens with yellow stripes on the leaf margins are associated with [[Ọya]], the female [[orisha]] of storms. In Nigeria, the plant is commonly linked with [[Ògún]], the orisha of war, and is used in rituals to remove the evil eye.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.org/details/a-la-recherche-des-plantes-perdues-les-plante-reouvees-par-les-descendants-cultur |title=A LA RECHERCHE DS PLANTES PERDUES, Les plante reouvées par les descendants culturels des Yoruba au Brésil |date=1 July 1995 |access-date=14 August 2020 |language=fr }}</ref>

In Brazil, where it is known as ''espada de São Jorge'' ("[[Saint George and the Dragon|Saint George's sword]]"),<ref name="Carlessi">{{cite journal |url=https://ojs.ethnobiology.org/index.php/ebl/article/view/1547/826 |title=How to Carry Out a Democratic Ethnobotanical Study |date=4 December 2019 |doi=10.14237/ebl.10.1.2019.1547 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814092647/https://ojs.ethnobiology.org/index.php/ebl/article/view/1547/826 |access-date=14 August 2020 |archive-date=14 August 2020 |language=en |last1=Carlessi |first1=Pedro Crepaldi |journal=Ethnobiology Letters |volume=10 |pages=113–119 |s2cid=209473075 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Melo">Aline Melo. [https://revistacasaejardim.globo.com/Casa-e-Jardim/Paisagismo/noticia/2020/10/espada-de-sao-jorge-lanca-de-sao-jorge-ou-espada-de-santa-barbara.html "Espada de São Jorge, lança de São Jorge ou Espada de Santa Bárbara?"] ''Casa e Jardim.'' 9 October 2020. Retrieved 10 February 2024. {{inlang|pt}} ''"No Brasil, popularizou-se o uso de três espécies: a ''[[Sansevieria trifasciata#Varieties and cultivars|Sansevieria zeylanica]]'', autêntica espada-de-são-jorge, verde e rajada; a ''Sansevieria trifasciata'', com bordas amareladas da raiz às pontas, que ficou conhecida como espada-de-santa-bárbara; e a ''[[Sansevieria cylindrica]]'', a lança-de-são-jorge, com aspecto pontudo e folhagens fechadas em formato cilíndrico."''</ref> it is grown outside houses to ward off evil that might harm the home (as is ''[[Dracaena angolensis]]'', Saint George's spear).<ref name="Melo"/> The plant plays an important part in the Afro-Brazilian syncretic religion [[Umbanda]],<ref name="Carlessi"/><ref name="Melo"/> also representing the orisha [[Ogum]] (Ògún),<ref name="Ah">Heloísa Von Ah. [https://www.wemystic.com.br/3-tipos-de-espada-de-sao-jorge-conheca-as-principais-diferencas/ "3 tipos de Espada-de-São-Jorge: conheça as principais diferenças."] WeMystic. Date not given. Retrieved 10 February 2024. {{inlang|pt }}</ref> as Ogum is syncretized with [[Saint George]]. Some yellow-edged varieties of ''D. trifasciata'' are called ''espada de Santa-Bárbara'' ("Sword of [[Saint Barbara]]") and are associated with [[Iansã]], the Umbanda name for Ọya, Saint Barbara's syncretic orisha pair.<ref name="Ah"/><ref name="Melo"/> These types are grown to protect against inclement weather.<ref name="Ah"/><ref name="Melo"/> 

This plant is visible on the porch in American [[Grant Wood]]'s 1930 painting, ''[[American Gothic]]''.<ref name="agh">{{cite web |website=American Gothic House Center |url=https://americangothichouse.org/american-gothic |title=The Painting - The Plants |access-date=11 July 2022 }}</ref><ref name="ching2019">{{cite journal |last=Ching |first=Barbara |title=Transplanted— Edward Hopper in Cedar Rapids, Grant Wood in New York City: A Review Essay |journal=The Annals of Iowa |pages=194–206 |volume=78 |issue=2 |date=2019 |doi=10.17077/0003-4827.12564 |s2cid=242816098 |url=https://pubs.lib.uiowa.edu/annals-of-iowa/article/id/12485/ |access-date=11 July 2022 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="biel2006">{{cite book |title=American Gothic: A Life of American's Most Famous Painting |chapter=Parody |pages=120–172 |last=Biel |first=Steven |date=2005 |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |isbn=9780393059120 }}</ref>
